name: Messianic Expectations and Apocalyptic Hopes

objectives.text: Identify that God promised to send a King to rescue his people and that many people were waiting for him
Recall that the words Messiah and Christ both mean anointed one and name Jesus as the promised Messiah
Retell how Simeon and Anna waited in the temple for the promised one and recognized the baby Jesus
Explain why many people expected the Messiah to defeat the Romans and why Jesus riding into Jerusalem on a donkey surprised them
Explain the title Son of David and connect it to God's covenant promise of an everlasting throne
Compare the popular hope for a warrior king with the suffering servant described in Isaiah
Describe how the Old Testament anointing of prophets, priests, and kings shaped the hope for a Messiah who would fulfill all three offices
Identify the hope of bodily resurrection at the end of the age in Daniel and in Martha's words to Jesus
Summarize how the Maccabean revolt and the later Roman conquest of Judea intensified political hopes for a deliverer
Distinguish canonical Scripture from intertestamental writings such as 1 Maccabees and 1 Enoch and explain how the Reformed tradition uses the latter as historical sources rather than as Scripture
Explain the main features of apocalyptic literature such as visions, symbolic beasts, cosmic conflict, and God's final triumph using examples from Daniel
Interpret the Son of Man figure in Daniel and analyze how Jesus applied the title to himself at his trial
Explain the Jewish framework of the present age and the age to come and identify where the New Testament uses it
Analyze how Daniel's seventy weeks prophecy fed first century expectations and how the Reformed tradition reads it as fulfilled in Christ
Compare the different figures first century Jews expected, including a Davidic king, a prophet like Moses, and a returning Elijah
Analyze the disciples' hope for the restoration of Israel's kingdom and how the risen Jesus responded to it
Examine accounts of revolutionary leaders such as Theudas and Judas the Galilean and explain what they reveal about popular messianic movements
Evaluate how Jesus redefined messiahship through suffering, death, and exaltation using the Gospel accounts and Isaiah's servant songs
Synthesize how Jewish hopes for resurrection, judgment, and new creation are taken up in the Reformed confession of Christ's return and the last things

changes: Kept and reworded real competencies: waiting for a King, Messiah as anointed one, the expectation of victory over Rome and the surprise of Jesus' humility, Son of David, warrior king versus suffering servant, resurrection hope, Son of Man, Daniel's prophecies, the age to come, the profile of expectations, Jesus' redefinition of messiahship, and the Jewish roots of eschatology. Dropped the filler objective about observing people praying and the speculative objective about Judas's motives. Recast the analysis of Enoch and Maccabees as distinguishing canon from intertestamental writings, anchored to WCF 1.3, and added a separate historical objective on the Maccabean and Roman setting. Added objectives on Simeon and Anna, the threefold office, the apocalyptic genre, the seventy weeks, the disciples' kingdom question, and first century revolutionary movements. Anchored the objectives to specific verses and confession articles, and left material on sects, the synagogue, and the feasts to the sibling sub-topics.
